item.content:encoded:
As a native speaker of Spanish I'd say that Drewbear is right.

On the other hand, in my own country (Spain) is quite common in colloquial speak to put the definite article before the name of a person. Here you could say "la Tía Carmela" - or even "la Carmela" - and no one would find it strange. I don't know how it works in the different countries of Latin America, though.

(sorry for the little rant)

item.content:encoded: But in this case she's not talking/thinking about "the grandmother"; she's referring to "Grandmother Maricela". I'm using it as a name signifier, like you might call your own grandparents "Nana" or "Gramps" or whatever. The el/la wouldn't be necessary in that case, I believe. It would be like saying "The FaustoV made a comment and the Drewbear replied."

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I liked it. I don't see anything in spanish here very often, so i feel this as a fresh air.

By the way, in spanish, qhen you are talking about somebody's action in third person, is really normal to put "el" or "la" (translated in english would be "The" before the subject. for example:

Abuela maricela said it would pass/ The Abuela maricela said it would pass.

Actually you did it correctly, but it feels better for me in the second way.

item.content:encoded: A bit of setting would help! I assume this village would be in the border with the U.S. or a little after. Normally the only words that do not get translated into english are the ones that name an object or a holiday otherwise untranslatable. Words like "Tía" or "muerto" can be translated with no problem.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The Foundation took all the bushes that that guy had. We know nothing about any other specimens, and I'm assuming that he couldn't have had all of them; plants have a way of escaping into the wild. :-P

As for the Latin America angle, I was actually thinking that it was Guatemala, which would have a higher, cooler climate closer to that that might be found in New Hampshire. I have friends that live there, and apparently they have enormous kite festivals on Dia de los Santos (same day, different name). I used Dia de los Muertos as the name so people would know that yes, this was supposed to be Halloween. Perhaps this village has a larger connection to Mexican customs than Guatemala at large. :-P

Okay so 324's article says it was originally found in New Hampshire, which is like very far away from Mexico (Since you said "village" and everybody's speaking Spanish, I assume we're in Mexico), and the Foundation took all the samples away, the only explanation I can think of is that the original 324 bush came from Mexico, which, aside from being one HELL of a transplant journey, isn't supported anywhere in the original article. I'm not against the idea, it's just a bit of a stretch with such little supporting documentation.

Even so, like I said I really like this tale.
